claims.text: Adding a minor amount of hafnium to a conventional boride-based component will improve its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Hafnium addition promotes in situ formation of a dense protective Hf-rich oxide scale.
The proposed baseline is an undoped conventional binary boride such as TiB2.
A low level of hafnium can be introduced during synthesis or by surface modification.
Standard hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure occurs at approximately 700–850 °C.
Hafnium modification will produce a continuous, refractory Hf-rich oxide, such as HfO2, along the component surface.
Substituted hafnium atoms promote oxidation during high-temperature exposure.
The resulting Hf-rich oxide barrier will be stable and adherent.
The Hf-rich oxide barrier limits diffusion of molten aluminum into the boride matrix.
Limiting aluminum diffusion retards corrosive attack on the boride.
Hf-doped boride will exhibit lower mass loss than undoped boride during molten-aluminum exposure.
Hf-doped boride will retain better surface integrity than undoped boride during molten-aluminum exposure.
Undoped boride components typically have higher corrosion rates under molten-aluminum exposure.
The protective effect should persist under standard hot-dip-plating temperatures and aluminum chemistries.
Performance under substantially different temperatures or nonstandard aluminum chemistries is uncertain.
The magnitude of corrosion reduction will depend on hafnium concentration and oxide-layer continuity.
A controlled comparison at approximately 750 °C can test Hf-doped samples against undoped samples under otherwise identical conditions.
Mass loss, corrosion rate, surface morphology, and surface composition can be used to evaluate corrosion and oxide-scale formation.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant mass-loss reduction or a continuous adherent Hf-rich oxide barrier would falsify the hypothesis.
